claim: Rod photoreceptors generate measurable responses to single-photon activation of individual molecules of rhodopsin.
source: Rod photoreceptors generate measurable responses to single-photon activation of individual molecules of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), rhodopsin.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by the citation context and experimental approach of the manuscript.

claim: Timely rhodopsin desensitization depends on phosphorylation and arrestin binding.
source: Timely rhodopsin desensitization depends on phosphorylation and arrestin binding, which quenches G protein activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rhodopsin phosphorylation has been measured biochemically at C-terminal serine residues.
source: Rhodopsin phosphorylation has been measured biochemically at C-terminal serine residues, suggesting that these residues are critical for producing fast, low-noise responses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical work.

claim: Serine-only rhodopsin generated prolonged step-like single-photon responses that terminated abruptly and randomly.
source: Contrary to expectation, serine-only rhodopsin generated prolonged step-like single-photon responses that terminated abruptly and randomly, whereas threonine-only rhodopsin generated responses that were only modestly slower than normal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Threonine-only rhodopsin generated responses that were only modestly slower than normal.
source: Contrary to expectation, serine-only rhodopsin generated prolonged step-like single-photon responses that terminated abruptly and randomly, whereas threonine-only rhodopsin generated responses that were only modestly slower than normal.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The step-like responses of serine-only rhodopsin reflect slow and stochastic arrestin binding.
source: We show that the step-like responses of serine-only rhodopsin reflect slow and stochastic arrestin binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Threonine sites play a privileged role in promoting timely arrestin binding and rhodopsin desensitization.
source: Thus, threonine sites play a privileged role in promoting timely arrestin binding and rhodopsin desensitization.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: All but a few GPCRs desensitize through phosphorylation by G protein receptor kinases (GRKs) followed by the binding of arrestin.
source: Nonetheless, all but a few GPCRs desensitize through a common set of reactions: phosphorylation by G protein receptor kinases (GRKs) followed by the binding of arrestin.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The >800 GPCRs expressed by humans are desensitized by only 7 GRKs and 4 arrestins.
source: Interestingly, the >800 GPCRs expressed by humans are desensitized by only 7 GRKs and 4 arrestins (Wilden et al., 1986; Lohse et al., 1990; Pitcher et al., 1998; Gurevich and Gurevich, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GPCR C-termini typically have multiple possible phosphorylation sites.
source: GPCR C-termini, where the desensitization reactions take place, typically have multiple possible phosphorylation sites (Krupnick and Benovic, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some phosphorylation sites are more rapidly phosphorylated than others.
source: Biochemical experiments indicate that some sites are more rapidly phosphorylated than others, for example, serine sites appear to be preferred in the case of the photopigment rhodopsin (Kennedy et al., 2001; Maeda, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical work.

claim: Serine sites appear to be preferred phosphorylation sites in rhodopsin.
source: Biochemical experiments indicate that some sites are more rapidly phosphorylated than others, for example, serine sites appear to be preferred in the case of the photopigment rhodopsin (Kennedy et al., 2001; Maeda, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical work.

claim: The pattern of phosphorylation sites can control the effect of arrestin binding on the receptor.
source: The pattern of phosphorylation sites can control the effect of arrestin binding on the receptor, that is, whether arrestin promotes receptor desensitization or internalization (Key et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2005; Butcher et al., 2011; Nobles et al., 2011; Shukla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Single-photon responses generated by vertebrate rods vary much less than expected from simple stochastic models for single molecules.
source: SPRs generated by vertebrate rods vary much less than expected from simple stochastic models for single molecules (Baylor et al., 1979; Rieke and Baylor, 1998; Whitlock and Lamb, 1999; Field and Rieke, 2002; Doan et al., 2006, 2009; Gross et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Low variability in single-photon responses requires precise control of the timing of rhodopsin desensitization.
source: This low variability requires precise control of the timing of rhodopsin desensitization (Mendez et al., 2000; Doan et al., 2006, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation and arrestin binding need to work in a coordinated fashion to minimize variability in rhodopsin activations.
source: In particular, phosphorylation and arrestin binding need to work in a coordinated fashion so as to minimize brief rhodopsin activations produced by too rapid arrestin binding and long rhodopsin activations produced by too slow arrestin binding.
evidence: This is supported by inference from previous work and the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Native serine sites are phosphorylated rapidly and begin to lower rhodopsin's catalytic activity.
source: Namely, native serine sites are phosphorylated rapidly and begin to lower rhodopsin's catalytic activity (Ohguro et al., 1993, 1994, 1995; Gibson et al., 2000; Mendez et al., 2000; Kennedy et al., 2001), but serine phosphorylation only weakly promotes arrestin binding; native threonine sites are phosphorylated more slowly but are essential to promote rapid arrestin binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Serine phosphorylation only weakly promotes arrestin binding.
source: Namely, native serine sites are phosphorylated rapidly and begin to lower rhodopsin's catalytic activity (Ohguro et al., 1993, 1994, 1995; Gibson et al., 2000; Mendez et al., 2000; Kennedy et al., 2001), but serine phosphorylation only weakly promotes arrestin binding; native threonine sites are phosphorylated more slowly but are essential to promote rapid arrestin binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Native threonine sites are phosphorylated more slowly but are essential to promote rapid arrestin binding.
source: Namely, native serine sites are phosphorylated rapidly and begin to lower rhodopsin's catalytic activity (Ohguro et al., 1993, 1994, 1995; Gibson et al., 2000; Mendez et al., 2000; Kennedy et al., 2001), but serine phosphorylation only weakly promotes arrestin binding; native threonine sites are phosphorylated more slowly but are essential to promote rapid arrestin binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: Transgenic mouse strains were backcrossed with Rho−/− mice so that rods expressed only a single type of rhodopsin.
source: Transgenic mouse strains were backcrossed with Rho−/− mice so that these rods expressed only a single type of rhodopsin (Lem et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Time-to-peak and peak amplitude of single-photon responses were not significantly different across rhodopsin types.
source: Time-to-peak and peak amplitude were not significantly different across rhodopsin types (p > 0.14, Kruskal–Wallis test, corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: T → A rhodopsin produced responses that plateau and then terminate abruptly.
source: In particular, T → A rhodopsin (Figure 1D) produced responses that plateau and then terminate abruptly.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: T → A responses plateau to a common level before terminating at random times.
source: Overlaying all SPRs gathered from a rod illustrates the extent of this effect (Figure 1G); whereas responses elicited by Rho or S → A rhodopsin follow similar trajectories, the T → A responses plateau to a common level before terminating at random times.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Response duration distributions are non-normal.
source: Response duration distributions are non-normal (p < 0.001, K-S test for non-normality) and are significantly different from one another at the 99% confidence level (Kruskal–Wallis analysis of variance, corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: For all rhodopsin types, the variance of single-photon responses peaked after the peak of the mean response.
source: For all rhodopsin types, the variance peaked after the peak of the mean response (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The peak in the variance of T → A responses coincides with the point at which approximately half of the responses have returned to baseline.
source: The T → A mutant is an extreme case of this effect: the peak in the variance of the T → A responses coincides with the point at which approximately half of the responses have returned to baseline (2.9 s, compare to median duration 2.7 s in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The time course of the variance suggests that a single desensitization step is greatly prolonged for T → A rhodopsin.
source: Thus, the time course of the variance suggests that a single desensitization step is greatly prolonged for T → A rhodopsin.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of variance data.

claim: CVarea for WT rods was 0.37 ± 0.02.
source: CVarea for WT rods (0.37 ± 0.02) was comparable to that found previously (Doan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: Responses of S → A rods had increased variability (CVarea = 0.51 ± 0.02).
source: Responses of S → A rods had increased variability (CVarea = 0.51 ± 0.02, Figure 2E)
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The CVarea for T → A responses was 0.78 ± 0.03.
source: The CVarea for the T → A responses (0.78 ± 0.03, Figure 2E) was much higher, consistent with a strong disruption of the normally reproducible timing of rhodopsin desensitization.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Isoelectric focusing showed that WT rhodopsin has eight bands, indicating unphosphorylated rhodopsin, opsin, plus six differently phosphorylated species.
source: Immunoblots of rhodopsin from solubilized WT retina samples showed eight bands, indicating unphosphorylated rhodopsin (0), opsin (0*) plus six differently phosphorylated species, consistent with previous results (Mendez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: T → A and S → A rhodopsin showed five bands in isoelectric focusing, corresponding to opsin, unphosphorylated, singly, doubly, and triply phosphorylated rhodopsin.
source: Blots of both T → A and S → A samples showed five bands, corresponding to opsin (0*) and unphosphorylated (0), singly (1), doubly (2), and triply (3) phosphorylated rhodopsin, showing that T → A and S → A mutants can be phosphorylated at all sites (Figure 3A,B, Mendez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: T → A mutant had higher levels of doubly and triply phosphorylated rhodopsin than S → A mutants.
source: Quantification of the intensity of the bands showed that the T → A mutant had higher levels of doubly and triply phosphorylated rhodopsin than the S → A mutants (Figure 3B, Mendez et al., 2000), a result consistent with previous observations that serine sites are more rapidly and efficiently phosphorylated than threonine sites (Ohguro et al., 1993, 1994, 1995; Kennedy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3B and supported by citations.

claim: Arrestin-1 was able to bind to T → A and S → A rhodopsin in purified outer segment disk membranes that had been phosphorylated by recombinant GRK1.
source: In addition to the finding that mutant rhodopsins can be phosphorylated, arrestin-1 was able to bind to T → A and S → A rhodopsin in purified outer segment disk membranes that had been phosphorylated by recombinant GRK1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of mutant receptors on an arrestin-1 knockout background prolonged responses.
source: As expected from the biochemical assay, the expression of mutant receptors on an arrestin-1 knockout background (Arr−/−) prolonged responses (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Termination of mutant rhodopsin activity requires arrestin-1.
source: the similarity of these prolonged responses to those of Rho/Arr−/− rods (Xu et al., 1997) indicates that termination of the mutant activity requires arrestin-1.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous work.

claim: The collecting area for S → A rods was 0.63 ± 0.04 μm2 or 1.3× the collecting area of WT rods.
source: The collecting area for S → A rods was 0.63 ± 0.04 μm2 or 1.3× the collecting area of WT rods (0.5 μm2, Azevedo and Rieke, 2011).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: 3D reconstruction of rods from serial electron micrographs showed that transgenic expression of T → A and S → A rhodopsin changed the size of rod outer segments.
source: 3D reconstruction of rods from serial electron micrographs showed that transgenic expression of T → A and S → A rhodopsin changed the size of rod outer segments (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The volume of S → A rods was 1.3× larger than WT rods.
source: The volume of S → A rods was 1.3× larger than WT rods (T → A rods had ∼0.75× the volume).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: T → A rods had ∼0.75× the volume of WT rods.
source: The volume of S → A rods was 1.3× larger than WT rods (T → A rods had ∼0.75× the volume).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data.

claim: S → A rods express ∼1.3× as much rhodopsin as WT rods, at the same concentration.
source: Thus, S → A rods express ∼1.3× as much rhodopsin as WT rods, at the same concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the collecting area and volume measurements.

claim: Differences between S → A and WT responses cannot be explained by changes in volume or rhodopsin expression level.
source: Thus, differences between S → A and WT responses cannot be explained by changes in volume or rhodopsin expression level.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of volume and expression data.

claim: The normalized average response of Combo rods could be fit by a weighted sum of the Rho (51%) and T → A responses (49%).
source: (1) The normalized average response of the Combo rods could be fit by a weighted sum of the Rho (51%) and T → A responses (49%) (Figure 5B), indicating that a near-equal mixture of the pure responses can explain the time course of the Combo rod responses.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The distribution of response durations from Combo rods was best fit by an equal mixture of the duration distributions from Rho and T → A rhodopsin.
source: (2) The distribution of response durations from the Combo rods (gray crosses in Figure 5C) was best fit by an equal mixture of the duration distributions from Rho and T → A rhodopsin (black line in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The kinetics of identified T → A-like and Rho-like responses from Combo rods agreed closely with the kinetics of the pure responses.
source: (3) The kinetics of identified T → A-like and Rho-like responses from Combo rods agreed closely with the kinetics of the pure responses (Figure 5D,E; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 'Materials and methods' for response identification).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: T → A rhodopsin produces responses with similar kinetics in either T → A or Combo rods.
source: In summary, Figure 5 shows that T → A rhodopsin produces responses with similar kinetics in either T → A or Combo rods, and WT rhodopsin produces responses with similar kinetics in either WT or Combo rods.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Combo rod data.

claim: WT, T → A, and Combo rods have similar transduction cascade kinetics.
source: These findings indicate that WT, T → A, and Combo rods have similar transduction cascade kinetics, and thus, that replacement of threonines causes the prolonged SPRs in T → A rods.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Combo rod data.

claim: Reduced arrestin-1 expression had little or no effect on S → A SPR kinetics or durations.
source: Reduced arrestin-1 expression had little or no effect on S → A SPR kinetics (Figure 6A,B, cyan trace) or durations (Figure 6C, cyan crosses).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Reduced GRK1 expression did not noticeably change S → A SPR kinetics or durations.
source: Reduced GRK1 expression similarly did not noticeably change SPR kinetics or durations (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: The rate of desensitization of threonine-only rhodopsin appears to be limited by phosphate attachment by bound GRK1 rather than GRK1 or arrestin-1 binding.
source: Among the reactions controlling rhodopsin desensitization (Figure 1A), only the rate of phosphate attachment is insensitive to GRK1 and arrestin-1 concentration. Hence, the rate of desensitization of threonine-only rhodopsin appears to be limited by phosphate attachment by bound GRK1 rather than GRK1 or arrestin-1 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing insensitivity to GRK1 and arrestin-1 concentration.

claim: Reducing the arrestin-1 concentration slowed the kinetics of the average T → A SPR.
source: Reducing the arrestin-1 concentration, however, slowed the kinetics of the average SPR (Figure 7B, cyan trace).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The median response duration of T → A/Arr1+/− rods increased by a factor of ∼1.5, from 2.7 s to 4.3 s.
source: Correspondingly, the duration distribution in T → A/Arr1+/− rods shifted to longer times (Figure 7C): the median ΔT (50% point on the y-axis) increased by a factor of ∼1.5, from 2.7 s to 4.3 s (Figure 7C,G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7C,G.

claim: Desensitization of T → A rhodopsin is slowed by reducing the arrestin-1 concentration.
source: Thus, desensitization of T → A rhodopsin is slowed by reducing the arrestin-1 concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing prolonged responses with reduced arrestin-1.

claim: Reducing the GRK1 concentration produced modest changes in the average T → A SPR and response duration.
source: Reducing the GRK1 concentration, however, produced modest changes in the average SPR (Figure 7E) and response duration (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: The sensitivity of T → A responses to reducing arrestin-1 and the relative insensitivity to reducing GRK1 implicates arrestin-1 binding as the slow step in desensitization of T → A rhodopsin.
source: The sensitivity of T → A responses to reducing arrestin-1 and the relative insensitivity to reducing GRK1 implicates arrestin-1 binding as the slow step in desensitization of T → A rhodopsin.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing effects of reducing arrestin-1 vs GRK1.

claim: The fastest response decay has a time constant ∼200 ms, similar to previous measurements of the rate of the G protein's GTPase activity.
source: First, the fastest response decay has a time constant ∼200 ms, similar to previous measurements of the rate of the G protein's GTPase activity (Krispel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8 and supported by citation.

claim: All termination-aligned responses share a fast decay time constant of ∼200 ms.
source: Three types of responses share this fast decay: (1) all termination-aligned responses (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The briefest flash-aligned responses have a fast decay time constant of ∼200 ms.
source: Three types of responses share this fast decay: (1) all termination-aligned responses (Figure 8B); (2) the briefest flash-aligned responses (Figure 8C; 0.5 s bin)
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The longest flash-aligned responses have a fast decay time constant of ∼200 ms.
source: Three types of responses share this fast decay: (1) all termination-aligned responses (Figure 8B); (2) the briefest flash-aligned responses (Figure 8C; 0.5 s bin); and (3) the longest flash-aligned responses (Figure 8C; 4 s bin).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Flash-aligned traces of intermediate kinetics have substantially slower decay time constants.
source: Flash-aligned traces of intermediate kinetics have substantially slower decay time constants (Figure 8D, τflash; bins between 1 s and 3 s).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Termination-aligned S → A responses exhibited recovery time constants near 200 ms.
source: Termination-aligned S → A responses also exhibited recovery time constants near 200 ms (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), matching those of termination-aligned responses from Rho and T → A rhodopsin.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: G protein decay dominates the kinetics of the fastest WT responses.
source: The analysis of Figure 8 suggests that G protein decay dominates the kinetics of the fastest WT responses, when, stochastically, rhodopsin is short-lived.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of response kinetics shown in Figure 8.

claim: The slower recovery of flash-aligned, intermediate-duration WT responses is consistent with a combination of slower rhodopsin desensitization and G protein decay.
source: The slower recovery of flash-aligned, intermediate-duration WT responses is consistent with a combination of slower rhodopsin desensitization and G protein decay.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of response kinetics shown in Figure 8.

claim: Phosphorylation of native serines is rapid but ineffective in promoting rapid arrestin-1 binding.
source: We found that phosphorylation of native serines is rapid but ineffective in promoting rapid arrestin-1 binding.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of native threonines is slow but effective in promoting rapid arrestin-1 binding.
source: Phosphorylation of native threonines is slow but effective in promoting rapid arrestin-1 binding.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Normal arrestin-1 binding was not recapitulated in vitro by substituting charged residues for native phosphorylation sites.
source: Interestingly, normal arrestin-1 binding was not recapitulated in vitro by substituting charged residues for native phosphorylation sites (Ling et al., 2004; Ascano and Robinson, 2006; Ascano et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rhodopsin with only three serine sites remaining (T → A) recovered with a mean duration of ∼4 s.
source: However, rhodopsin with only three serine sites remaining (T → A) recovered with a mean duration of ∼4 s (Figure 2A), more than five times faster than responses from rhodopsin with only two serine sites remaining (S334/S338) (Doan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and compared to previous work.

claim: The addition of a single serine (at position 343) substantially speeds the response, likely because of faster arrestin-1 binding.
source: Thus, the addition of a single serine (at position 343) substantially speeds the response, likely because of faster arrestin-1 binding (Figure 7; Vishnivetskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: Serine sites promote arrestin-1 binding, albeit much less effectively than threonine sites.
source: This suggests that serine sites promote arrestin-1 binding, albeit much less effectively than threonine sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing serine and threonine mutants.

claim: Threonine sites are more slowly phosphorylated than serine sites.
source: This is consistent with biochemical experiments indicating that threonine sites are more slowly phosphorylated than serine sites (Ohguro et al., 1993, 1994, 1995; Kennedy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical work.

claim: Maximizing the affinity of arrestin-1 binding has been found to require four or more phosphates.
source: Maximizing the affinity of arrestin-1 binding has been found to require four or more phosphates, suggesting that phosphorylation of at least one threonine is necessary for normal desensitization (Vishnivetskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Regardless of where threonines are located in the C-terminal sequence, their presence leads to comparable degrees of receptor quenching in a cell-free assay.
source: It also appears that regardless of where threonines are located in the C-terminal sequence, their presence leads to comparable degrees of receptor quenching in a cell-free assay (Brannock et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The somatostatin subtype 2A receptor is phosphorylated at serine sites to a greater extent than at threonine sites.
source: Other GPCRs can function in a similar manner: the somatostatin subtype 2A receptor is phosphorylated at serine sites to a greater extent than at threonine sites (Hipkin et al., 1997), but threonine phosphorylation is required for normal desensitization (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Threonine phosphorylation is required for normal desensitization of the somatostatin subtype 2A receptor.
source: Other GPCRs can function in a similar manner: the somatostatin subtype 2A receptor is phosphorylated at serine sites to a greater extent than at threonine sites (Hipkin et al., 1997), but threonine phosphorylation is required for normal desensitization (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The asymmetric role of threonine and serine sites may be a general mechanism tuning the affinity and binding kinetics of arrestin.
source: Thus, the asymmetric role of threonine and serine sites may be a general mechanism tuning the affinity and binding kinetics of arrestin, controlling timely and reproducible desensitization of GPCR activity, and determining which intracellular pathways are activated.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and comparison to other GPCRs.

claim: Arrestins are composed of a C-domain and an N-domain, connected by a 12-residue 'hinge' region.
source: Arrestins are composed of a C-domain and an N-domain, connected by a 12-residue 'hinge' region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about arrestin structure.

claim: The two domains of arrestin are normally held fixed by the interaction of the arrestin C-terminus with the N-domain and the polar core.
source: These two domains are normally held fixed by the interaction of the arrestin C-terminus with the N-domain and the polar core, a network of charges paradoxically buried within the protein (Granzin et al., 1998; Hirsch et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work.

claim: The phosphorylated C-terminus of the GPCR is suspected to disrupt the polar core of arrestin.
source: The phosphorylated C-terminus of the GPCR is suspected to disrupt the polar core, freeing the C-terminus and gate loops (Hirsch et al., 1999; Gurevich and Gurevich, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Rhodopsin's native threonine sites more readily interact with arrestin's polar core to 'activate' arrestin.
source: In the context of this model, our results suggest that rhodopsin's native threonine sites more readily interact with arrestin's polar core to 'activate' arrestin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of arrestin structure.

claim: Arrestin's '139 loop' is a critical mediator of selectivity for phosphorylated rhodopsin.
source: Other recent evidence points to arrestin's '139 loop' as a critical mediator of selectivity for phosphorylated rhodopsin (Vishnivetskiy et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A crystal structure of arrestin-2 together with a phosphorylated C-terminus peptide from the V2R receptor shows that a critical lysine in the 'middle loop' is coordinated with a phosphate.
source: A crystal structure of arrestin-2 (β-arrestin-1) together with a phosphorylated C-terminus peptide from the V2R receptor shows that a critical lysine in the 'middle loop' (139 loop) is coordinated with a phosphate (Shukla et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: The arrangement of rhodopsin's C-terminal phosphorylation sites is important for interaction with arrestin.
source: In this model, our data indicate that the arrangement of rhodopsin's C-terminal phosphorylation sites is important for this interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in the context of arrestin structure.

claim: Rhodopsin's effective lifetime in mouse rods has been a matter of debate.
source: Rhodopsin's effective lifetime in mouse rods has been a matter of debate: some studies support fast rhodopsin desensitization, such that G protein decay determines the rate of response recovery (Krispel et al., 2006; Gross and Burns, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work showing different findings.

claim: Some studies support fast rhodopsin desensitization, such that G protein decay determines the rate of response recovery.
source: Rhodopsin's effective lifetime in mouse rods has been a matter of debate: some studies support fast rhodopsin desensitization, such that G protein decay determines the rate of response recovery (Krispel et al., 2006; Gross and Burns, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Other studies find that the rate of rhodopsin desensitization is sufficiently slow to affect the rate of response recovery.
source: Other studies find that the rate of rhodopsin desensitization is sufficiently slow to affect the rate of response recovery (Doan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Under the experimental conditions used, rhodopsin activity is occasionally short-lived but often persists sufficiently long to shape the SPRs.
source: The results of Figure 8 indicate that, under our experimental conditions, rhodopsin activity is occasionally short-lived but often persists sufficiently long to shape the SPRs (see also Baylor et al., 1984).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of response kinetics shown in Figure 8.

claim: On average the kinetics of rhodopsin desensitization are closely matched to the kinetics of the transduction cascade.
source: This suggests that on average the kinetics of rhodopsin desensitization are closely matched to the kinetics of the transduction cascade.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of response kinetics.

claim: Replicating the measured low variability of the response requires 6–7 steps.
source: Assuming that the transduction cascade acts linearly to convert rhodopsin activity to changes in current, replicating the measured low variability of the response requires 6–7 steps (Doan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Non-linearities in the transduction process could reduce the number of steps required to explain low variability.
source: Non-linearities in the transduction process could reduce the number of steps required (Bisegna et al., 2008; Gross et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: Multiple events must work in a concerted fashion to control rhodopsin desensitization.
source: nonetheless, a shared feature of all current explanations for reproducibility is that multiple events must work in a concerted fashion to control rhodopsin desensitization.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from previous modeling work.

claim: Arrestin-1 binding must be coordinated with phosphorylation so that it does not occur too quickly or too slowly.
